Chapter Six: The Hive Switch—How We Become “Groupish” and Transcend Ourselves
Have you ever felt that spark of magic when you’re swept up in a crowd? Maybe it’s the electricity of voices singing together at a concert, or the effortless teamwork of a group all moving toward the same goal. Sometimes it’s the way a room fills with energy during a shared ritual or a powerful song. In those moments, you might notice your sense of self starting to blur, replaced by a strong feeling of belonging. That’s what the author calls the “hive switch.” It’s this deep, almost ancient ability to become “groupish”—to actually feel and act as if you’re part of something much bigger than just yourself.
Most days, we move through life focused on our own needs and wants. But sometimes, when the right conditions line up, something shifts inside us. Suddenly, the group’s needs feel just as important as our own. There’s this rush of unity and shared purpose—sometimes even awe, joy, or a sense of transcendence. It’s almost like our minds are built not just for looking out for ourselves, but for thriving together.
This groupish instinct isn’t some odd quirk. It’s actually a huge part of why our societies work. Way back in history, groups that could cooperate—really come together—had a big advantage over those that couldn’t. Things like rituals, synchronized movements, and powerful symbols helped people bond, making them more willing to sacrifice for the common good. We still see it all the time: military drills, sports chants, or even just friends gathering around a dinner table. These are all ways we flip that hive switch, creating closeness and trust.
There’s a great story from the book about volunteers coming together after a natural disaster. At first, everyone’s just focused on their own tasks, quietly getting things done. But as the day goes on, something changes. People start watching out for each other, sharing snacks and encouragement, even cracking jokes to lighten the mood. By the end, there’s this deep sense of connection—almost like, for just a moment, everyone was part of something larger, something that truly mattered.
Of course, the hive switch isn’t all sunshine. The same power that unites a group can also turn outsiders into “them.” When people feel fused with their group, empathy for others can fade, sometimes even turning into hostility. History has plenty of examples where this groupishness led to exclusion, conflict, or even violence.
But here’s the thing: the hive switch reminds us of what’s possible when people come together. Morality isn’t just about our own choices—it’s also about the ties that bind us to each other. Most of us don’t realize just how much our sense of meaning and purpose comes from these moments of collective unity.
So, what can we do with this knowledge? When we understand the hive switch, it becomes clearer why we’re drawn to groups, to rituals, and to bigger causes. It’s also a chance to build bridges—to create opportunities for shared experiences and real cooperation. If we can find ways to flip that hive switch together, even with people who are different from us, who knows what new kinds of connection and understanding we might discover?
